title: Should You Write Names On The Board To Keep Track Of Consequences? ep-track-of-consequences/
author: Michael Linsin
summary: Linsin argues against the long-standing practice of writing misbehaving students' names on the board to track consequences, calling it humiliating and unnecessarily public. He contends the practice functions as an additional, unofficial consequence on top of whatever the management plan calls for, and that it exposes students' struggles to visiting parents, colleagues, and administrators who have no need to know. As an alternative, he recommends a private clipboard roster with a column per day, where teachers mark dots or lines for rule violations, filed monthly and available for parent conferences or administrative review without any public exposure. He shares his own early-career discomfort with the whiteboard method as reinforcing the argument for a quieter system.

quotes: Having your name written up for the world to see for an entire day can be humiliating.
This, in turn, can have a negative effect on your relationship with misbehaving students , as well as your ability to influence and motivate them to improve their behavior.
Parents who stop by your classroom, and even other teachers, shouldn’t be able to see (or gossip about) who is struggling or having a bad day.
Just attach a roster with enough columns for an entire month, and simply make dots or lines in the appropriate box for every time a student breaks a rule.
It felt as if I were marking students with a scarlet letter or handing them a dunce cap to wear.
It’s just pure accountability, which results in true reflection and the intrinsic desire within the student not to make the same mistake again.
